terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where Idris's price list asks the store room for paper on your docket.

tasks.title: Keep or fail a docket
tasks.description:
Implement the constructor of `Docket` in `src/docket.js`.

- `new Docket(executor)` calls `executor` once, right away, with two functions: `resolve` and `reject`
- until one of them is called, `state` is `'pending'` and `value` is `undefined`
- `resolve(value)` keeps the docket: `state` becomes `'fulfilled'` and `value` is that very value, whatever it is, even when `resolve` is called long after the constructor returned
- `reject(reason)` fails it: `state` becomes `'rejected'` and `value` is that very reason

The check makes dockets of its own, calls `resolve` and `reject` now and later, and reads `state` and `value`.
nextSteps: Run `node src/price-list.js` and read the error.
Make two small functions inside the constructor, one that keeps the docket and one that fails it.
Run the script again: card should be pending at first. The script still stops at the smudged count; that is task 3.
hints: The constructor does not know the value. The executor will find it, now or later, and needs a way to hand it back.

A function made inside the constructor can still change `this.state` and `this.value` when it is called later, from anywhere, because it remembers the docket it was made in. Arrow functions keep `this` as it was where they were written.
`executor((value) => { this.state = 'fulfilled'; this.value = value }, (reason) => { ... })` is the shape. Fill in the second one the same way.

tasks.title: Settle once and only once
tasks.description:
Make a docket settle only once. After the first call to `resolve` or `reject`, every later call to either one does nothing: it does not change `state` or `value`, and it does not throw.

This holds whatever the first value was, `undefined` included.

The check calls `resolve` and `reject` on its own dockets in every order, several times, and reads `state` and `value` after each.
nextSteps: Look at the posters line in the price list: it calls resolve twice.
Find the one place that every call to resolve and reject goes through.
Decide there whether the docket is still waiting.
Run the script: the posters should keep their first count.
hints: A docket is a promise about one outcome. Once there is an outcome, a second one would mean two people read two different answers off the same docket.
What tells you a docket has settled? Not its value: a docket kept with `undefined` has settled all the same.
Start both functions with `if (this.state !== 'pending') return`. It is simplest when both call one shared function that does the check once.

tasks.title: An executor that throws
tasks.description:
When the executor throws, the docket fails with exactly what was thrown, and `new Docket` itself does not throw.

- this holds for anything thrown: an `Error`, a string, even `undefined`
- a throw after the executor already called `resolve` or `reject` changes nothing, as in task 2

The check makes dockets whose executors throw values of every kind, some after settling, and reads `state` and `value`.
nextSteps: Look at the smudged count in the price list.
Find where the constructor calls the executor.
Catch what it throws and fail the docket with it.
Make sure a throw after settling goes through the same rule as task 2.
hints: Code that makes a docket expects a docket back, not a crash. A throw in the executor is just another way of saying it failed.
`try { ... } catch (error) { ... }` catches anything thrown inside the `try`, including from a function you call there. Decide by being in the `catch`, not by looking at what was caught.
Wrap the executor call in a `try`, and in the `catch (error)` call the same function your `reject` uses, so a docket that already settled stays as it is.
